title: Periodic table: chemical periodicity
objectives: Describe and explain the variations across Period 3 in atomic radius, ionic radius, melting point and electrical conductivity, in terms of structure and bonding
Explain the variation in first ionisation energy and electronegativity across Period 3
Describe the reactions of the Period 3 elements with oxygen, chlorine and water
State and explain the variation in the oxidation number, structure, bonding and acid–base behaviour of the oxides and chlorides of Period 3
Describe the reactions of the oxides with water and with acids and bases, and of the chlorides with water, including the pH of the solutions
Predict the properties of an element in Period 3 from its position, and deduce the identity of an element from given information
why: Period 3 is where all your physical chemistry comes together: the same ideas of nuclear charge, bonding and structure explain why sodium is a soft metal, silicon a hard semiconductor and chlorine a gas, and why their oxides go from strongly basic to strongly acidic. Periodicity questions appear on almost every Paper 1 and are a favourite Paper 2 data question.
intro: Going across Period 3 from sodium to argon, the elements change from metals to non-metals. This chapter tracks the physical properties of the elements, then the chemistry of their oxides and chlorides, and finally how to use these patterns to identify unknown elements and predict properties.

blocks.name: period3
blocks.title: Period 3 explorer
blocks.h: Switch between properties to see the trends as a bar chart, and click an element for its structure, its reaction with water, and its oxide and chloride.
Atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl: the nuclear charge increases by one each time, but electrons go into the same (third) shell with similar shielding, so they are pulled closer.

items: Cations (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) are much smaller than their atoms: they have lost the third shell. They get smaller across (same 2,8 arrangement, more protons).
Anions (P³⁻, S²⁻, Cl⁻) are larger than their atoms: extra electrons, more repulsion. They get smaller across (same 2,8,8, more protons).
So every anion is larger than every cation in the period.

blocks.title: Melting points of the Period 3 elements

blocks.h: First ionisation energy generally increases (greater nuclear charge, smaller radius), with dips at Al (electron removed from the higher-energy 3p sub-shell) and S (removing one of a pair of 3p electrons, which repel). Electronegativity increases steadily from Na to Cl for the same reasons.

blocks.q: Why does sulfur have a higher melting point than phosphorus?
o: S has more covalent bonds per atom
S₈ molecules have more electrons than P₄, so stronger id-id forces
blocks.why: Both are simple molecular. S₈ (128 electrons) has stronger id-id forces than P₄ (60 electrons).

S + O₂ → SO₂ (blue flame); SO₂ → SO₃ needs a catalyst

blocks.h: The highest oxidation number in the oxides equals the number of outer-shell electrons: +1 (Na₂O), +2, +3, +4, +5 (P₄O₁₀), +6 (SO₃). In the chlorides it goes +1 to +5 (PCl₅).

items: basic: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O; Na₂O + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O
acidic: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O (hot, concentrated); P₄O₁₀ + 12NaOH → 4Na₃PO₄ + 6H₂O; SO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O

blocks.h: The pattern follows electronegativity: metal oxides with large electronegativity differences are ionic and basic; non-metal oxides are covalent and acidic; aluminium sits in between and is amphoteric.

blocks.wrong: SiO₂ is a basic oxide because it does not dissolve in water.
blocks.right: Insolubility says nothing about acid–base nature. SiO₂ reacts with NaOH, not with acids: it is acidic.

blocks.h: Ionic chlorides dissolve; covalent chlorides are hydrolysed (react with water), producing HCl, which makes the solution strongly acidic and gives misty (steamy) fumes in moist air.

blocks.title: pH of the solution when each chloride is added to water

blocks.q: Explain why molten MgCl₂ conducts electricity but liquid SiCl₄ does not.
blocks.a: MgCl₂ is ionic: in the melt its ions can move and carry charge. SiCl₄ consists of neutral covalent molecules, so there are no mobile charged particles.

blocks.h: Exam questions often give clues (conductivity, melting point, behaviour of the oxide or chloride with water, pH, a formula) and ask you to identify elements. Work through each clue, eliminate, and check every option against all the clues.

items: Conducts and reacts vigorously with cold water → Na.
Oxide dissolves in both acid and alkali → Al.
Very high melting point, semiconductor, chloride is a liquid that leaves a white solid with water → Si.
Oxide gives an acidic solution and chloride is hydrolysed with no solid → P (or S for the oxide).
Chloride dissolves to give pH 6.5 and Mg(OH)₂ with NaOH → Mg.

blocks.title: Mystery compound
blocks.h: Read the clue and pick the oxide or chloride that fits. Ten mysteries, shuffled each round.

blocks.q: Element E is in Period 3. Its oxide has a giant structure and does not react with water or dilute acids, but dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH. Its chloride is a liquid. Identify E and write an equation for the chloride with water.
blocks.err: Choosing Al: Al₂O₃ also reacts with acids, and AlCl₃ is a solid.

summary: Atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl: more protons, same shell, similar shielding.
Cations are smaller than their atoms (lost a shell); anions are larger (extra electron repulsion).
Na, Mg, Al: giant metallic, conductivity and melting point rise with delocalised electrons per atom.
Si: giant covalent, highest melting point, semiconductor. P₄, S₈, Cl₂, Ar: simple, low melting, non-conductors.
First IE generally rises across, with dips at Al (3p) and S (paired 3p); electronegativity rises steadily.
Highest oxidation number in oxides: +1 (Na₂O) to +6 (SO₃); equals the number of outer electrons.
Oxides: Na₂O, MgO basic (ionic); Al₂O₃ amphoteric; SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃ acidic (covalent).
Na₂O → NaOH pH 14; MgO → pH 9; Al₂O₃, SiO₂ insoluble; P₄O₁₀ → H₃PO₄ pH 2; SO₃ → H₂SO₄ pH 1.
Chlorides: NaCl, MgCl₂ ionic, dissolve (pH 7, 6.5). AlCl₃, SiCl₄, PCl₅ covalent, hydrolysed to HCl (pH 2–3).

flash.q: Trend in atomic radius across Period 3 and why?
flash.a: Decreases: nuclear charge increases, same shell, similar shielding

flash.q: Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point and why?
flash.a: Si: giant covalent, many strong bonds

flash.q: Why does Al conduct better than Na?
flash.a: Al gives 3 delocalised electrons per atom, Na only 1

flash.q: Why is P₄’s melting point low?
flash.a: Simple molecular: only id-id forces between molecules

flash.q: Where does first IE dip in Period 3?

flash.a: Reacts with both acids and bases

flash.q: pH when Na₂O is added to water?
pH of NaCl and MgCl₂ solutions?
Highest oxidation number of S in its oxides?
Which Period 3 chloride is a liquid that leaves a white solid with water?

practice.q: Explain the trend in melting point from Na to Al.
practice.a: Increases: number of delocalised electrons per atom rises (1, 2, 3) and the ions are smaller with higher charge, so metallic bonding gets stronger.

practice.q: Write equations for the reactions of MgO with HCl, and of SO₃ with NaOH.
practice.a: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O; SO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O

practice.q: Describe what you would see when water is added dropwise to solid PCl₅, and give the pH of the final solution.
practice.a: Vigorous reaction, steamy (misty) fumes of HCl, solid disappears to give a colourless solution; pH about 1–2.

practice.q: Explain why Al₂O₃ is amphoteric while Na₂O is basic, using electronegativity.
practice.a: Na and O have a large electronegativity difference: purely ionic, O²⁻ acts as a base. Al is more electronegative, so Al₂O₃ has covalent character and can react with bases too.

practice.q: An element X burns to form a white oxide that dissolves in water to give pH 2. Its chloride, XCl₅, fumes in moist air. Identify X and give the equation of the oxide with water.
Arrange Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻ and S²⁻ in order of increasing radius. Explain.
practice.a: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻. Cations have two shells, anions three; within each pair, the one with more protons is smaller.

assessment.q: Which Period 3 element has the largest atomic radius?
assessment.why: Lowest nuclear charge with three shells.

assessment.q: Which element has a giant covalent structure?
What is the pH of the solution when SO₃ is added to water?
Which chloride dissolves in water without hydrolysis?
What forms when SiCl₄ is added to water?
Which has the highest melting point?
assessment.why: 933 K: strongest metallic bonding of these.

assessment.q: Highest oxidation number of phosphorus in its oxides?
Which element reacts vigorously with cold water?
What is the acid–base nature of SiO₂?
Approximate pH of AlCl₃ in water?

assessment_s.q:
This question is about magnesium and phosphorus and their oxides and chlorides.
(a) Write equations for the reaction of each element with an excess of oxygen. [2]
(b) Describe and explain the difference in the melting points of MgO and P₄O₁₀. [2]
(c) Write an equation for the reaction of each oxide with water and give the pH of each solution. [3]
assessment_s.a:
(a) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; P₄ + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀
(b) MgO much higher: giant ionic lattice with strong attraction between ions; P₄O₁₀ is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces
(c) MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂, pH about 9; P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄, pH about 2

assessment_s.q:
Element Z is in Period 3. Z is a poor conductor of electricity and has a melting point of 1687 K.
(a) Identify Z and describe its structure and bonding. [2]
(b) Z reacts with chlorine. Write the equation and describe what happens when the product is added to water. Include an equation. [3]
(c) Predict, with a reason, whether the oxide of Z reacts with dilute HCl. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) silicon; giant covalent (macromolecular) lattice, each Si bonded to four others
(b) Si + 2Cl₂ → SiCl₄; fumes of HCl and a white solid; SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl
(c) no: SiO₂ is an acidic oxide (it reacts with bases, not acids)

pp.skill: Recognising the trend in electronegativity
pp.mis: Confusing it with ionisation energy, which has dips
pp.stem: Which property increases at every step from Na to Cl, with no dips?
pp.exp: Electronegativity rises steadily (Na 0.9 → Cl 3.2). First IE dips at Al and S; melting point peaks at Si; conductivity rises to Al then falls to almost zero.

pp.skill: A property that changes in one direction across Period 3
pp.mis: Choosing a property with a peak
pp.stem: Which property decreases for each successive element from Na to Cl?
opts: number of electrons in the outer shell
pp.exp: Nuclear charge rises while electrons go into the same shell with similar shielding, so the atoms get smaller at every step.

pp.skill: Identifying a property from its pattern across consecutive elements
pp.mis: Not matching the pattern to the peak at silicon
pp.stem: Five consecutive Period 3 elements, V to Z (in order of atomic number), have these values of a property: V 371, W 923, X 933, Y 1687, Z 317. Which row identifies the property and element Y?
opts: first ionisation energy / kJ mol⁻¹; aluminium
pp.exp: A big rise to a peak and a sudden drop is the melting-point pattern: Na 371, Mg 923, Al 933, Si 1687 (giant covalent), P 317 (simple molecular). Y is silicon.

pp.skill: Ordering melting points across Period 3
pp.mis: Forgetting that phosphorus melts below sodium
pp.stem: What is the order of melting points of Na, Al, P and Si, from lowest to highest?
pp.exp: P₄ (317 K, simple molecular) < Na (371 K, weak metallic) < Al (933 K, 3 delocalised electrons per atom) < Si (1687 K, giant covalent).

pp.skill: Explaining the melting points of silicon and phosphorus
pp.mis: Saying covalent bonds break when phosphorus melts
pp.stem: Why does phosphorus melt at a much lower temperature than silicon?
opts: Phosphorus has weaker covalent bonds between its atoms.
Phosphorus is a simple molecular solid; only weak id-id forces between P₄ molecules are overcome.
Phosphorus atoms are larger than silicon atoms.
pp.exp: Silicon is giant covalent: melting breaks many strong Si–Si bonds. Phosphorus melts without breaking the P–P bonds inside the P₄ molecules.

pp.skill: Combining melting point and conductivity trends
pp.mis: Assuming the highest melting element always conducts best
pp.stem: In which set of three elements does one element have both the highest melting point and the highest electrical conductivity of the three?
pp.exp: Al melts highest (933 K) of Na, Mg, Al and has the most delocalised electrons per atom, so it conducts best. In B and C, Si melts highest but conducts poorly; in D, S melts highest but does not conduct.

pp.skill: Comparing Period 3 properties
pp.mis: Assuming IE always rises from one element to the next
pp.stem: Which statement is correct?
opts: The atomic radius of phosphorus is larger than that of magnesium.
Sulfur has a higher melting point than silicon.
Aluminium has a higher first ionisation energy than magnesium.
Aluminium has a higher electrical conductivity than magnesium.
pp.exp: Al gives 3 delocalised electrons per atom, Mg gives 2. P is smaller than Mg; Si (giant covalent) melts far higher than S; Al’s first IE is lower than Mg’s (3p electron).

pp.skill: Identifying elements from melting point and conductivity
pp.mis: Thinking every conductor melts high
pp.stem: X, Y and Z are Period 3 elements. Which row identifies them?
opts: X magnesium; Y silicon; Z phosphorus
X silicon; Y magnesium; Z phosphorus
X magnesium; Y phosphorus; Z silicon
X sodium; Y silicon; Z sulfur
pp.exp: X conducts and melts at 650 °C: Mg (Na melts at 98 °C). Y melts very high and is a semiconductor: Si. Z melts at 44 °C and does not conduct: white phosphorus (S melts at 115 °C).

pp.skill: Interpreting a data table for Period 3 elements
pp.mis: Mixing up the reasons for high and low melting points
pp.stem:
Use the data for the Period 3 elements (Na to Ar: m.p. / K 371, 923, 933, 1687, 317, 388, 172, 84; Na, Mg, Al good conductors, Si poor, P to Ar non-conductors).
1 Every element with a simple molecular structure melts below 400 K.
2 Silicon conducts poorly because it has very few mobile electrons.
3 Magnesium melts lower than sodium.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: 1: P₄, S₈, Cl₂ and Ar all melt below 400 K. 2: Si is a semiconductor with few delocalised electrons. 3: false: Mg 923 K > Na 371 K.

pp.skill: Relating melting point to electronegativity across Mg to P
pp.mis: Expecting melting point to rise with electronegativity throughout
pp.stem: For Mg, Al, Si and P, melting point is plotted against electronegativity. Which description of the graph is correct?
opts: the points rise steadily from left to right
the points rise from Mg to Si, then fall sharply at P
the points fall steadily from left to right
Mg has the highest melting point and P the lowest electronegativity
pp.exp: Electronegativity increases Mg < Al < Si < P, so the points go left to right in that order. Melting point rises to Si (giant covalent), then drops to P (simple molecular).

pp.skill: Atomic v ionic radius for a metal and a non-metal
pp.mis: Thinking ions keep the order of their atoms
pp.stem: Magnesium and chlorine form MgCl₂. How do the atomic and ionic radii of magnesium compare with those of chlorine?
opts: atomic: Mg larger; ionic: Mg²⁺ larger
atomic: Mg larger; ionic: Cl⁻ larger
atomic: Cl larger; ionic: Cl⁻ larger
atomic: Cl larger; ionic: Mg²⁺ larger
pp.exp: Across the period, atoms shrink, so Mg > Cl. Mg²⁺ has lost its outer shell (2,8) while Cl⁻ has 2,8,8, so Cl⁻ is much larger.

pp.skill: Deducing elements from the sizes and electrons of their ions
pp.mis: Forgetting that metal ions in Period 3 have 10 electrons
pp.stem: X and Y are Period 3 elements; Y has the larger atomic number. The stable ion of X is larger than the stable ion of Y, and Y’s ion has 10 electrons. Which row is correct?
opts: electrons in X’s ion: 10; larger atomic radius: X
electrons in X’s ion: 10; larger atomic radius: Y
electrons in X’s ion: 18; larger atomic radius: X
electrons in X’s ion: 18; larger atomic radius: Y
pp.exp: Y’s ion has 10 electrons, so Y is a metal (Na, Mg or Al). X comes earlier in the period, so X is also a metal with a 10-electron ion (larger because of lower nuclear charge). Earlier in the period means a larger atom: X.

pp.skill: Using atomic and ionic radii to deduce properties
pp.mis: Assuming a larger ion means a non-metal
pp.stem: X and Y are Period 3 elements. X has a larger atomic radius than Y, and the common ion of X is also larger than the common ion of Y. Both ions have 10 electrons. Which statement is correct?
opts: X has a lower first ionisation energy than Y.
The oxide of Y is acidic.
X has a greater atomic number than Y.
Y forms a chloride that is a liquid at room temperature.
pp.exp: Both are metals (10-electron cations), and X comes before Y (e.g. Na and Mg). Earlier in the period → lower nuclear charge → lower first IE. Their oxides are basic or amphoteric and their chlorides are solids.

pp.skill: Interpreting atomic and ionic radius data
pp.mis: Not noticing which ion is larger than its atom
pp.stem: Atomic and ionic radii (nm) of three Period 3 elements: X 0.143 and 0.053; Y 0.104 and 0.184; Z 0.186 and 0.102. Which statement is correct?
opts: X has a higher melting point than Z.
Y is a good electrical conductor.
The oxide of Z is amphoteric.
X has a larger atomic radius than Z.
pp.exp: Ions smaller than atoms → metals; Y’s ion is larger → non-metal (S). Z (largest atom) is Na; X is Al. Al melts at 933 K, Na at 371 K. Na₂O is basic; S does not conduct.

pp.skill: Identifying an element from the pH of its oxide in water
pp.mis: Thinking all metal oxides dissolve
pp.stem: A Period 3 element burns in oxygen to form a white solid. The solid reacts with water to give a solution of pH 13–14. What is the element?
pp.exp: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, a strongly alkaline solution. Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ do not react with water; SO₂/SO₃ give acidic solutions.

pp.skill: Acid–base nature and structure of an oxide
pp.mis: Linking “metal oxide” with “simple molecular”
pp.stem: What are the acid–base nature and structure of magnesium oxide?
pp.exp: MgO is an ionic oxide of a metal: giant ionic lattice and basic (reacts with acids; gives Mg(OH)₂, pH about 9, with water).

pp.skill: Properties of the oxides of Na, Mg and S
pp.mis: Calling MgO amphoteric
pp.stem: Which row about the oxides Na₂O, MgO and SO₃ is correct?
opts: Na₂O basic; MgO basic; SO₃ acidic
Na₂O basic; MgO amphoteric; SO₃ acidic
Na₂O giant ionic; MgO giant ionic; SO₃ giant covalent
Na₂O low m.p.; MgO high m.p.; SO₃ high m.p.
pp.exp: Na₂O and MgO are basic, giant ionic, high-melting. SO₃ is simple molecular (melts at 17 °C) and acidic (forms H₂SO₄).

pp.skill: Reactions of oxides with water
pp.mis: Thinking SiO₂ dissolves to give an acid
pp.stem: Which row describes the reactions of Na₂O, P₄O₁₀ and SiO₂ with water?
opts: Na₂O forms NaOH(aq); P₄O₁₀ forms H₃PO₄(aq); SiO₂ no reaction
Na₂O no reaction; P₄O₁₀ forms H₃PO₄(aq); SiO₂ forms H₂SiO₃(aq)
Na₂O forms NaOH(aq); P₄O₁₀ no reaction; SiO₂ no reaction
all three react to form acidic solutions
pp.exp: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (pH 13–14). P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄ (pH about 2). SiO₂ is insoluble (giant covalent), though it is still an acidic oxide.

pp.skill: Oxides that react with acid but not alkali
pp.mis: Thinking MgO is amphoteric
pp.stem: Which oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid but not with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
pp.exp: MgO is basic only. Al₂O₃ is amphoteric (reacts with both); SO₂ and P₄O₁₀ are acidic (react with NaOH).

pp.skill: Identifying an oxide from its state and acidity
pp.mis: Forgetting which oxides are gases
pp.stem: At room temperature, one Period 3 oxide is a colourless gas with a choking smell; its aqueous solution turns blue litmus red. Which is it?
pp.exp: SO₂ is a gas: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃. P₄O₁₀ is a white solid; Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are high-melting solids.

pp.skill: Explaining melting points of two oxides
pp.mis: Explaining by oxidation number
pp.stem: Magnesium oxide melts at 2852 °C; sulfur trioxide melts at 17 °C. Which statement explains this?
opts: Mg has a lower oxidation number than S.
MgO is giant ionic; SO₃ is simple molecular.
Metallic character decreases across the period.
pp.exp: Melting MgO breaks strong ionic bonding throughout the lattice; melting SO₃ overcomes only weak intermolecular forces.

pp.skill: Statements about the periodicity of oxides
pp.mis: Thinking SiO₂ is simple molecular
pp.stem:
Three statements about the Period 3 oxides are given.
1 The highest oxidation number in the oxides rises from +1 (Na₂O) to +6 (SO₃).
2 Na₂O and MgO are basic and Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.
3 The oxides from Si to S are all simple molecular.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: 1 and 2 are correct. SiO₂ is giant covalent, so 3 is false.

pp.skill: Substances that lower the pH of an alkaline solution
pp.mis: Forgetting that some salts remove OH⁻
pp.stem: Sodium is added to water to make an alkaline solution. Which two substances could each lower the pH when added to it?
pp.exp: MgCl₂ removes OH⁻ as Mg(OH)₂ precipitate; P₄O₁₀ is an acidic oxide and neutralises OH⁻. NaCl has no effect; Na₂O and MgO are basic.

pp.skill: Balancing equations for burning Period 3 metals
pp.mis: Not checking every coefficient
pp.stem: Three equations: 1 xAl + yO₂ → zAl₂O₃; 2 xMg + yO₂ → zMgO; 3 xNa + yO₂ → zNa₂O. Which can be balanced with x = 4 and y = 1?
pp.exp: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (y = 1). 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ needs y = 3. 4Mg + 2O₂ → 4MgO needs y = 2.

pp.skill: Which chloride is not hydrolysed
pp.mis: Thinking every chloride gives HCl with water
pp.stem: Which chloride does not produce HCl when added to water?
pp.exp: NaCl is ionic and simply dissolves (pH 7). AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₅ are hydrolysed, releasing HCl.

pp.skill: What happens when PCl₅ is added to water
pp.mis: Expecting a precipitate
pp.stem: Which describes what happens when phosphorus(V) chloride is added to water?
opts: It dissolves to give a neutral solution.
It reacts vigorously, giving steamy fumes and an acidic solution with no precipitate.
It reacts to give a white precipitate and a neutral solution.
pp.exp: PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl. Both products are soluble acids (pH about 2); HCl fumes. (SiCl₄ gives a white precipitate of SiO₂.)

pp.skill: Correct statements about chlorides
pp.mis: Thinking strong covalent bonds stop hydrolysis
pp.stem: Which statement is correct?
opts: Silicon tetrachloride is a giant covalent solid.
An aqueous solution of sodium chloride has a pH of about 2.
Strong Si–Cl bonds prevent SiCl₄ from reacting with water.
When aluminium chloride is added to water, the resulting solution is acidic.
pp.exp: AlCl₃ is hydrolysed to give an acidic solution (about pH 3). SiCl₄ is a simple molecular liquid that reacts readily with water. NaCl(aq) is neutral.

pp.skill: Explaining the pH of chloride solutions
pp.mis: Calling MgCl₂ fully hydrolysed
pp.stem: The chloride of element A dissolves in water to give a solution of pH 6.5. The chloride of element B reacts with water to give a white solid and a solution of pH 2. Which statement is correct?
opts: A is magnesium and B is silicon.
A is phosphorus and B is sodium.
A’s chloride is covalent and B’s is ionic.
pp.exp: MgCl₂ is ionic and dissolves, only very slightly hydrolysed (pH about 6.5). SiCl₄ is covalent and hydrolysed: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl.

pp.skill: Identifying a chloride from test results
pp.mis: Missing the clue from the precipitate in excess NaOH
pp.stem: A white solid chloride of a Period 3 element dissolves in water to give a solution of pH about 6.5. Adding NaOH(aq) gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. What is the chloride?
pp.exp: pH 6.5 and a white precipitate (Mg(OH)₂) insoluble in excess NaOH: MgCl₂. Al(OH)₃ would dissolve in excess; NaCl gives no precipitate; PCl₅ gives pH about 2.

pp.skill: Identifying an element from its chloride’s reaction with water
pp.mis: Confusing Al and Si observations
pp.stem: A Period 3 element forms a liquid chloride. Water reacts with it vigorously, giving steamy fumes and a white solid that does not dissolve in dilute HCl. What is the element?
pp.exp: SiCl₄ (a liquid) + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl. SiO₂ does not dissolve in acid. AlCl₃ is a solid and Al(OH)₃ would dissolve in acid; PCl₅ gives no solid.

pp.skill: Identifying two compounds from a flow of tests
pp.mis: Mixing up the amphoteric and basic hydroxides
pp.stem: L is NaCl or MgCl₂. M is PCl₅ or SiO₂. L(aq) gives a white precipitate with a few drops of NaOH(aq), which does not dissolve in excess. M reacts with water to give steamy fumes and an acidic solution with no solid left. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: NaCl gives no precipitate with NaOH, so L is MgCl₂. SiO₂ does not react with water, so M is PCl₅.

pp.skill: Structure of Period 3 chlorides
pp.mis: Thinking all chlorides are ionic
pp.stem: Which chloride has a giant structure?
pp.exp: MgCl₂ is giant ionic (m.p. 714 °C). SiCl₄, PCl₃ and S₂Cl₂ are simple covalent molecules and liquids at room temperature.

pp.skill: Spotting inconsistent observations
pp.mis: Trying to force one identity on contradictory data
pp.stem: A student records these observations for the chloride of a Period 3 element: white crystalline solid; dissolves in water giving a solution of pH 1; does not melt until heated strongly above 700 °C. What can be deduced?
opts: At least one observation is wrong.
pp.exp: pH 1 means a covalent chloride hydrolysed by water, but covalent Period 3 chlorides melt (or boil) at low temperatures. A very high melting point means an ionic chloride, which gives pH 6.5–7. The observations contradict each other.

pp.skill: Identifying an element from its oxide and chloride
pp.mis: Forgetting that Al₂O₃ is amphoteric
pp.stem: Element Q is a metal. Its oxide dissolves in both dilute HCl and NaOH(aq), and its chloride fumes in moist air. Which element is Q?
pp.exp: Amphoteric oxide (Al₂O₃) and a chloride that is hydrolysed by water vapour (AlCl₃): aluminium.

pp.skill: Identifying three elements from their oxides and chlorides
pp.mis: Not using all three tests
pp.stem: X: oxide insoluble in water but reacts with both acids and alkalis; chloride hydrolyses. Y: oxide gives a weakly alkaline solution; chloride dissolves to give pH about 6.5. Z: oxide reacts with water to give an acidic solution; chloride hydrolyses to give pH about 2. Which row is correct?
opts: X Al; Y Mg; Z P
X Mg; Y Na; Z Si
X Al; Y Na; Z Mg
X Si; Y Mg; Z Al
pp.exp: Amphoteric oxide → Al. Weakly alkaline oxide and near-neutral chloride → Mg. Acidic oxide that reacts with water and a hydrolysed chloride → P.

pp.skill: Combining clues to identify three Period 3 elements
pp.mis: Mixing up liquid chlorides
pp.stem: W reacts vigorously with cold water to give an alkaline solution. X forms a liquid chloride that is hydrolysed, leaving a white solid. Y forms an oxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis. Which row is correct?
opts: W Na; X Si; Y Al
W Mg; X P; Y Al
W Na; X Al; Y Si
W Mg; X Si; Y Na
pp.exp: Vigorous reaction with cold water: Na (Mg reacts only very slowly). Liquid chloride leaving SiO₂: SiCl₄. Amphoteric oxide: Al₂O₃.

pp.skill: Deducing elements from formulae and ratios
pp.mis: Forgetting the formula of aluminium chloride
pp.stem: X is silicon or phosphorus. Its oxide reacts with water to give H₃XO₄. Y is magnesium or aluminium. 2 mol of Y react exactly with 3 mol of Cl₂. What are X and Y?
pp.exp: H₃PO₄ comes from P₄O₁₀ (SiO₂ does not react with water). 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ (Mg would need 1 : 1).

pp.skill: Identifying elements in a binary compound from its reactions
pp.mis: Not tracking the oxidation number of the oxide
pp.stem: Compound X contains two Period 3 elements, Y and Z. With water it forms a slightly soluble hydroxide and a hydride of Z. The hydride burns in air to form an oxide in which Z has an oxidation number of +4, and water. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: Slightly soluble hydroxide → Mg(OH)₂ (NaOH is very soluble). Oxide with Z at +4 from a hydride → SiH₄ → SiO₂. X is Mg₂Si.

pp.skill: Using trends to identify elements and their compound
pp.mis: Forgetting argon has the highest first IE
pp.stem: Y has the largest atomic radius in Period 3. Z has the second highest first ionisation energy in Period 3. What is the compound of Y and Z?
pp.exp: Largest atom: Na. Highest first IE is Ar; second highest is Cl. Na and Cl form NaCl.

pp.skill: Formula of a compound from clues about two elements
pp.mis: Choosing the wrong metal
pp.stem: X is the Period 3 metal with the highest melting point. Y is the Period 3 non-metal that forms a 2− ion. What is the formula of the compound of X and Y?
pp.exp: Of Na, Mg and Al, aluminium melts highest (933 K). Y is sulfur (S²⁻). Al³⁺ and S²⁻ → Al₂S₃.

pp.skill: Consecutive elements from IE and conductivity
pp.mis: Forgetting the dip at aluminium
pp.stem: Q, R and S are consecutive Period 3 elements. R has a lower first ionisation energy than both Q and S, and R is a good electrical conductor. What are Q, R and S?
pp.exp: First IE dips at Al (3p electron) and at S (paired 3p electron). Only Al conducts, so R = Al: Mg, Al, Si.

pp.skill: Trends in atomic radius and chloride pH
pp.mis: Getting the direction of the pH trend wrong
pp.stem: From sodium to phosphorus, how do the atomic radius of the element and the pH of the solution formed by its chloride with water change?
pp.exp: Atoms get smaller across the period. NaCl gives pH 7, MgCl₂ about 6.5, AlCl₃ about 3, SiCl₄ and PCl₅ about 2.

pp.skill: Checking pairs of statements about Period 3
pp.mis: Accepting one correct statement when both must be
pp.stem: In which row are both statements correct?
opts: Na is less electronegative than Cl. | Na₂O(aq) has a higher pH than SO₃(aq).
Al has a higher first IE than Mg. | MgO melts lower than Na₂O.
Si conducts better than Al. | SiO₂ is acidic.
P is a larger atom than Na. | P₄O₁₀ is basic.
pp.exp: A: both true. B: Al’s IE is lower than Mg’s, and MgO (2852 °C) melts higher than Na₂O. C: Al conducts far better than Si. D: both false.

pp.skill: General statements about Na to P
pp.mis: Overgeneralising hydrolysis or structure
pp.stem: Which statement about the Period 3 elements Na to P and their compounds is correct?
opts: All their chlorides are hydrolysed by water to give HCl.
The atomic radius increases as the nuclear charge increases.
All the elements have giant structures.
Only the oxides of Na and Mg give solutions with pH above 7 in water.
pp.exp: Na₂O and MgO are the only basic oxides that give alkaline solutions; Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble and P₄O₁₀ is acidic. NaCl is not hydrolysed; radius decreases; P₄ is simple molecular.

pp.skill: Oxidation numbers, oxides with water and amphoteric behaviour
pp.stem: This question is about the oxides of the Period 3 elements.

parts.q: State and explain the variation in the highest oxidation number of the elements in their oxides from Na₂O to SO₃.
ms: rises from +1 to +6
equals the number of outer-shell electrons used in bonding to oxygen

parts.q: Write equations for the reactions of Na₂O and P₄O₁₀ with water, and suggest the pH of each solution.
ms: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, pH 13–14
P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄
pH about 2

parts.q: State what is meant by amphoteric.
ms: reacts with (behaves as) both an acid and a base

parts.q: Write equations to show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
ms: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄

pp.skill: Bonding, structure and behaviour of Period 3 chlorides
pp.stem: The chlorides of the Period 3 elements show a trend in properties.

parts.q: Complete the information for NaCl, AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₅: type of bonding, type of structure, and approximate pH when added to water.
ms: NaCl: ionic, giant, pH 7
AlCl₃: covalent (in the vapour/dimer Al₂Cl₆), simple, pH about 3; SiCl₄: covalent, simple, pH about 2
PCl₅: covalent, simple (molecular), pH about 2

parts.q: Write an equation for the reaction of SiCl₄ with water.
ms: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl

parts.q: Explain why molten MgCl₂ conducts electricity but liquid SiCl₄ does not.
ms: MgCl₂ is ionic: in the melt the ions are free to move
SiCl₄ is made of neutral molecules: no ions or delocalised electrons

pp.skill: Radii, melting points and conductivity across Period 3
pp.stem: The Period 3 elements show trends in physical properties.

parts.q: Describe and explain the trend in atomic radius from Na to Cl.
ms: decreases
nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell (similar shielding), so they are pulled closer

parts.q: Explain why Na⁺ is smaller than a Na atom, but Cl⁻ is larger than a Cl atom.
ms: Na⁺ has lost its outer (third) shell
Cl⁻ has an extra electron in the same shell: more repulsion, same nuclear charge

parts.q: Explain why silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3 and phosphorus a low one.
ms: Si: giant covalent; many strong covalent bonds must be broken
P: simple molecular P₄; only weak id-id forces between molecules

parts.q: Explain why the electrical conductivity increases from Na to Al.
ms: number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3)

pp.skill: Oxides and chlorides of phosphorus compared with aluminium oxide
pp.stem: Aluminium oxide and phosphorus(V) oxide are both white solids. Phosphorus also forms PCl₃ and PCl₅.

parts.q: Al₂O₃ melts at 2072 °C and P₄O₁₀ at 340 °C. Explain the difference in terms of structure and bonding.
ms: Al₂O₃: giant (ionic, with some covalent character); strong bonds throughout must be broken
P₄O₁₀: simple molecular; weak intermolecular forces overcome

parts.q: State the oxidation number of phosphorus in PCl₃ and in PCl₅.
ms: +3 and +5

parts.q: Write an equation for the reaction of PCl₅ with an excess of water and state the approximate pH of the solution.
ms: PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl
pH about 1–2
